title: When two safety functions share a cause
goals: See that two headings which depend on the same basic event do not fail independently.
Predict the frequency of "both fail" first, then compare it with the exact value and with the product of the two failure probabilities.
assumptions: All numbers are made up for teaching. The initiating event happens 0.5 times per year. A shared support system S fails with probability 0.1. Injection fails if S fails or the injection pump fails (0.2). Cooling fails if S fails or the cooling pump fails (0.3). The tool treats S as ONE event used by both headings. The end states you name are examples, not conditions of any real plant. A frequency here is a result of this model under these assumptions, not a plant figure.

prediction.prompt: Before you analyse: how often per year do you expect BOTH headings to fail? Type your guess. There is no wrong guess; you will see it next to the result.

steps.prompt: Set the frequency of the initiating event to 0.5 per year.
steps.hint: Use the Frequency field under "Initiating event".

steps.prompt: Make heading 1 fail when X ("Injection fails") occurs and name it Injection. Make heading 2 fail when Y ("Cooling fails") occurs and name it Cooling.
steps.hint: X and Y are gates of the model. Both of them contain the basic event S, so both headings can be caused by the same failure.

steps.prompt: Type your prediction in the box "Your prediction" in the lesson panel.
steps.hint: You can reason with the numbers in the assumptions: how likely is each heading to fail on its own, and what would you get by multiplying?

steps.prompt: Give every sequence an end state. One end state for all of them is enough for this lesson.
steps.hint: Use "Give them all" above the Sequences table, or the list in each row.

outcomes.label: Injection and Cooling share the support system S

mistakes.message: Two headings fail on the same event. Injection is the gate X and Cooling is the gate Y.
TOP is the event that both fail at once. A heading is ONE safety function: use X for Injection and Y for Cooling, and let the tree work out what happens when both fail.
A frequency of 0 makes every sequence frequency 0. The initiating event happens 0.5 times per year here.

hand_calculation: Injection fails with probability P(X) = 1 - (1 - 0.1)(1 - 0.2) = 0.28. Cooling fails with probability P(Y) = 1 - (1 - 0.1)(1 - 0.3) = 0.37.
The product of the two, 0.28 x 0.37 = 0.1036, would be right only if the headings were independent. They are not: when S fails, both fail together.

Exactly: both fail if S fails, or if S works and both pumps fail. 0.1 + 0.9 x 0.2 x 0.3 = 0.154. Times 0.5 per year that is 0.077 per year; the product would give 0.0518 per year, about a third too low.

The other sequences: both work 0.9 x 0.8 x 0.7 = 0.504 (0.252 per year); Injection fails and Cooling works 0.9 x 0.2 x 0.7 = 0.126 (0.063 per year); Injection works and Cooling fails 0.9 x 0.8 x 0.3 = 0.216 (0.108 per year). The four probabilities add up to 1.

discussion.question: Which of the two numbers would you have trusted without the shared support system in the picture: the product, or the exact value? Why is the product too low?
discussion.answer: The product treats the failures as unrelated. S makes them travel together, so "both fail" is more likely than the product says.

discussion.question: In the model, how does the tool know the two headings share S?
discussion.answer: Both headings refer to gates of ONE fault-tree model, and S is one basic event inside both gates. If the author had drawn two separate events called S1 and S2, the tool would have treated them as unrelated.

discussion.question: Which assumption of this lesson would you most want to check for a real system?
discussion.answer: Independence of the basic events other than S, and whether S really is the only shared cause. Neither can be checked by the tool.
